utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. Case number IT-95-9-T, the Prosecutor versus Blagoje Simic, Miroslav Tadic, and Simo Zaric.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. We'll continue with the examination-in-chief. Mr. Pantelic, your witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes. Good afternoon, Your Honours. I'm just checking whether I am receiving B/C/S translation on channel 6. No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: We also need assistance with the laptop for Judge Williams.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Can I check whether I can receive on channel 6. No. No, I don't hear anything. Oh, it's okay. Now it's okay. Thank you. Sorry, Your Honour, for this small inconvenience. Your Honour, the Defence was informed about certain adjustments of time with regard to the limits. I would like to reiterate my position at the beginning of the Defence case. That was the first day when I said that the Defence is very mindful about the time-consuming issue, and personally the Defence for Mr. Blagoje Simic will take all necessary steps in order to limit or to restrict wherever it's possible. So in totality, I would like to say that we are going on a -- on a good track, I would say, and then with your permission, Your Honour, if for some witnesses there would be a small adjustment near the limited hours or little bit more, I would like to have your opinion whether we could proceed on that way, because as I said, in totality, for example, if we -- we have a plan for one witness to have a stand here for three hours or four hours and maybe he will be here for two hours, then in totality everything would be okay. It's very hard to predict, Your Honour, for each particular witness how -- how the things will go. So I hope that this flexible approach would be appropriate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Pantelic. The Trial Chamber will be as flexible as possible to allow the Defence to put their case forward.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Mr. Lukic. We are continuing now after the break. And before the break, the last topic we touched upon was the time period around mid-April in Samac and the events that you spoke about. I am now interested in hearing whether you know about a certain meeting which was held in the municipal premises sometime in mid-April, perhaps a few days after the breakout of the conflict. There were representatives of the neighbouring municipalities present, representatives from political parties, and so on. Were you present at that meeting, and if not, please tell us what you heard about it and just tell us in general what you know about it.

utterances.speaker: MIRKO LUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good afternoon to everybody. I would like to say that I remember that on the 15th of April, sometime in the morning hours, there was a meeting held in the premises of the municipal assembly -- or rather, the conference room, which was right across the office where I worked. I noticed that a large number of people were entering the conference room. I knew some of them. I didn't know all of them. And in the meantime, my inspectors and I were completing some tasks regarding tax declarations and so on. And when the meeting started -- I have to tell right away that I wasn't present at the meeting, but as I walked up and down the corridor, I stopped by the secretary's office, the Secretary of the President of the Assembly, and I asked her what was the agenda, what was that meeting about in the municipal building. And she told me that the president of the municipal assembly, Mr. Mito Banovic, convened a meeting at which, if I remember well, representatives of Orasje, Gradacac, Samac, Modrica and Odzak municipalities were supposed to be present, together with the representatives of the army. I saw several officers entering the conference room. I saw them passing through the corridor. So that means that there were some people there representing the army as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: If you could just go slower because of the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: MIRKO LUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Please tell me, Mr. Lukic, were there -- was there an increased number of soldiers around the municipal building? Were they armed? Could one notice a large military presence there?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO LUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have to tell you that after about an hour or hour and a half I left my office and went into town and I didn't notice anybody in the corridor, nor in front of the municipal building.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: We need to make a correction. Transcript page 3, line 13, there's a name here, Mito Banovic, but you in fact mentioned the president of the municipality.

utterances.speaker: MIRKO LUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The name was Mato Nuic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: And that is --

utterances.speaker: MIRKO LUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is the president of the Municipal Assembly of Bosanski Samac.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: And he's a Croat, a member of the HDZ, isn't he?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO LUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Now, please tell me, did you perhaps notice an argument or some kind of a noise, or was there an increased tension there during the meeting? I'm asking you this because your office was right across the hall from the conference room.

utterances.speaker: MIRKO LUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I didn't hear any noise, although I passed through the corridor, but I didn't hear any noise raised in the conference room. I didn't hear it.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Later on, after that meeting, in various talks that you had, did you perhaps learn more details about what transpired there at the meeting and what was discussed there?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO LUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I went home, and I didn't talk to anybody about that meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Please tell me, on the 16th of April you went to work, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO LUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Can you please describe that day for us. What happened then?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO LUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, on the 16th -- or rather, that entire month of April my inspectors and I were completing tax returns from the taxpayers and I remember that we worked on that day and that the inspector Dusan Mijanic and I were completing some tax returns, and we were in my office sometime until 12.30, until the afternoon hours. Then we went out into town to have a break and we went into a coffee-shop to have coffee. We went to a coffee-shop where we, municipal employees, went frequently. The coffee-shop was called Tri Jagode. We had coffee there and it was already almost 2.30, and I left the cafe. I intended to go home, but I had to go back to the municipal building because my car had been there. And as I came into the street that led to the municipal building, I met my colleague Ilija Tomic, and he asked me how I was doing, and I told him that I was tired and I went to the coffee-shop to have coffee and then I was heading home for lunch. And then he asked me where my wife and children were, and I was surprised. Why would he inquire about them? So I asked him about that, and he said, "Well, I have some information that there could be some commotion tomorrow." And I asked him, "What kind of commotion?" And he said, "I'm not quite sure but I heard something and it might be a good idea to take your wife and children out of town." Since I have two young children, I was quite taken aback by this. And when I came into the municipal building, saw that there was no Mercedes there and later I learned that the president of the municipality had driven it off and there was a Lada missing as well, and later I heard that it was driven away by Mato Madzarevic and another vehicle was missing and it became all quite strange to me -- it seemed strange to me. It was almost 4.00 at the time. I came home and I told my wife that things looked suspicious to me, and I suggested to my wife that perhaps she -- I could take her and the children out of town for some 10 days, just so -- to see what was going to happen and to see whether there was going to be any trouble or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: I have to interrupt you. Let us just clarify this, your colleague, Ilija Tomic, I assume was your colleague from the Internal Revenue Agency, wasn't he?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO LUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. He was employed by the Secretariat for Economy. But he's my colleague because he's a fellow lawyer. He worked on expropriations in the Secretariat for Economy.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: And this Ilija Tomic is what by ethnicity? And if you can, please go a bit slower.

utterances.speaker: MIRKO LUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He is a Croat by ethnicity, and he hails from Prud.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: And president of the municipality, Mr. Mato Nuic, a Croat, had his own official vehicle, a Mercedes, didn't he?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO LUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He had a black Mercedes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: And the Municipal secretary for economy, Mr. Mato Madzarevic, is a Croat, isn't he?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO LUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He was secretary for economy.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Therefore, both Mr. Nuic and Mr. Madzarevic had at their disposal municipal vehicles, didn't they?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO LUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Secretary for economy had a Lada vehicle. I don't remember the license plate. Whereas, the president of the municipality had a Mercedes at his disposal.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: When you had that conversation, did your colleague Ilija Tomic mention what kind of commotion could break out in the following days?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO LUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. He didn't specify that. He took me by surprise with that kind of news because prior to that we already had some trouble in our town, so I didn't ask him anything else in addition to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: When you say that prior to that there had been some trouble, what do you have in mind?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO LUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sijekovac and everything else that took place there.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: All right. You can continue, and tell us what happened afterwards, after that conversation you went home and what happened then? But please, if you can, relate that slower so that we can assist the interpreters. Please tell us how it was after that. You went home to see your family, and that was sometime in the evening hours, wasn't it? Tell us what time it was approximately.

utterances.speaker: MIRKO LUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was around 3.00 p.m. I came home and told my wife that I had received this news from Mr. Tomic, whom she knew as well, and then I said that it would perhaps be a good idea to take them to Serbian Negotin, because this was the only place where I had my family living, so I suggested that I should take her to Negotin. However, I've only visited that place some two or three times before. This is where my wife's sister lived, and I wasn't quite familiar with the road to Negotin. And then I called my brother-in-law --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Can you lead the witness such that he gives essential facts.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Sure, Your Honour. Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: We don't need all these details; they are taking your time.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Just essential facts about what happened, what he did, not all these details.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: So you called your brother-in-law, that is, your sister's husband -- your sister-in-law's husband. What was he by profession?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO LUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was a police officer in the Public Security Station in Bosanski Samac. He was an active policeman.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: And briefly, when you told him what your intention was, what did he tell you in reply?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO LUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He said, "What kind of commotion? I don't have any information about any kind of commotion, and I don't have any intention of taking the children."

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: So after that, you consulted again with your family, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO LUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: So what did you decide?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO LUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I told my wife that my brother-in-law doesn't want to go, so perhaps we shouldn't go either. Then she called her brother, and because he also has small children, and asked him whether he would be prepared to go to Negotin. And he responded, "Yes, and perhaps it wouldn't be bad for the women to go with the children for about ten days, and then we would bring them back."

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: So when did you leave for Negotin? What time was that?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO LUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We got some clothes ready for my wife and for the children, and then sometime around 7.00 p.m. -- 6.30 or 7.00 p.m. we left for Negotin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: When did you arrive at Negotin?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO LUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Around 2.00 a.m.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: What day was that?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO LUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was the morning of the 17th.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: When did you return to Samac?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO LUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We returned -- we spent the night there, and on the 17th at about 8.30 in the morning I woke up, I called the municipality to let them know that I will not be going to work that day. However, nobody picked up the phone in the municipal building, not even the executive board's president or the secretary seemed to be there. Then I called my house, and my father told me, "The Croats have knocked down the bridge at Hasici, you cannot pass through, and there is shooting in the direction of Samac." So at about 9.30 we left Negotin to go back home, the two of us, and we returned at about 6.30 or 7.00 in the early evening, that's when we returned home to Samac. I returned to my village, to Gornja Slatina, and he returned to Brnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: And this bridge that was destroyed at Hasici, how far is that bridge from -- how far is the place, Hasici, away from Samac?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO LUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: About 7 and a half kilometres in the direction of Gradacac.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: And when you came to your house that evening, did you find out any more about what went on that morning in Samac and in that region? Who did you meet there at your house, and what did you find out about the events of that night? And please slow down.

utterances.speaker: MIRKO LUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I returned to my house, not far from the house were my neighbours, who were all gathered there in one place. I asked them what was going on, and they said that they were called from the unit to be on the alert and not to go anywhere, and that's where they were. It was some kind of duty. They were on call and they were told that they would receive additional instructions later.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: So your neighbours were in uniforms and they belonged to some military unit.

utterances.speaker: MIRKO LUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. They belonged to the detachment. I think that that was the 6th Detachment.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Very well. So did you go to Samac that evening, in the evening of the 17th?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO LUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, because -- since I did have a wartime assignment from before, I decided that in case of an emergency situation, my place was to be in the municipality building in the post of the director of the Internal Revenue Agency. So with all of that in mind, I decided to go back to my place of work.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: And when you went to your workplace, what time was it approximately?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO LUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the morning of the 18th, at around 7.00, I went to Crkvina and there I reported to the command of the 2nd Detachment. That was the headquarters of the 2nd Detachment. I went there to ask what the situation was in the town and where I could find the president of the executive board.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Who did you talk to in that command of the 2nd Detachment, as you call it?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO LUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that that's where Marko Tubakovic was, also Juso Micic, Mirko Vasiljevic, and there were some other people. There were a large number of persons there, Rade Gunjevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Well, it's okay. You don't need to go into so many details. And where did you go after Crkvina?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO LUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They told me that it wasn't safe to move around town and that I should report to Pik because that is where the executive board president was is that it wasn't possible to get to the municipal building because there was shooting from the Croat side and it wasn't safe and there was nobody in the municipal building. Their messenger took me to Pik, and we asked where Mirko Jovanovic was sitting. There were soldiers around, and they indicated a room upstairs where Mirko was. I found Mirko there in the office upstairs of the administrative building of the agricultural industrial combine Samac.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: So what was Mr. Jovanovic's function?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO LUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mirko Jovanovic was the president of the executive board of the Municipal Assembly of Bosanski Samac.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Who was with Samac, if you remember, that day at Pik?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO LUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the meantime, Dako Misic came. He was one of the directors in the agricultural industrial plant. He stopped by, because I was sitting in his office. And then after a couple of hours, Milan Simic came, and he also sat down with us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Excuse me. Could we have a clarification, line 21 of page 11. It reads, and I also heard the same thing over the headset as well: "Who was with Samac, if you remember," which clearly doesn't make sense.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: We need to make a slight correction here in the transcript. I asked you who was with Mirko Jovanovic at Pik that day, and then you said that --

utterances.speaker: MIRKO LUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Dako Misic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Dako or Darko?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO LUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Dako.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Very well. After that you said Milan Simic came.

utterances.speaker: MIRKO LUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Was anyone else present there together with Mirko Jovanovic?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO LUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That day, no, there wasn't anybody else there.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: And what did you talk about?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO LUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We discussed the situation a little bit. I wanted him to tell me what the situation was and that we needed to urgently work on a plan to normalise the situation in the town, because people were afraid and a lot of people were in their basements because you could hear shooting. There were women and children in the basements and we needed to see how to organise life. We needed to see what to do with the civilian protection and to bring the situation as much as we could back to some kind of normal level. Then Mirko came and said, "We need to make some quick decisions first."

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: When you say "civilian protection," for the transcript, you're thinking of the civil protection service; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO LUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: And which measures did you personally and others undertake in order to resolve the issues relating to the civilian population?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO LUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, we set out first to find out what the major problem was, what the biggest problem was, and we determined that the biggest problem was the lack of bread. And since there were also children around, there was no milk, so we made some kind of plan, a very brief plan with only a few points on it. And since I knew that milk was being collected in the territory of the municipality to collection centres and from those centres it was being taken to the milk production plant, I organised that they deliver the milk directly from there and also to start the bakery working so that the civilian protection could distribute milk and bread to the population, because they did probably have some other essential foodstuffs at home. They had some kind of reserve supply.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: And tell me, did you yourself go around the town that day?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO LUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: How long did you stay in Samac?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO LUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That day, the 18th, in the afternoon around 6.00 p.m., perhaps I went home and then again I came to work the next day at 7.00 a.m. And using a loudspeaker -- and I know this because I remember seeing a vehicle that was calling people to come out through the loudspeaker to take the milk. They were asking them to come out of their apartments or to come out from the basements.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Was there any shelling of Samac? Did any shells fall on Samac that day?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO LUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Are you asking me about the 18th?

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MIRKO LUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but the shelling was not intense.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: If you know, which direction did the shells come from?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO LUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They came from quite close by, from the Croat side, I think from perhaps the area of Slavonski Samac, across the Sava River.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Were there any problems initially with water and electricity supplies?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO LUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: During the first few days, no. But then later the electricity was cut, because we were supplied with electricity from the Tuzla hydroelectric powerplant and they cut off the lines. So automatically then there was a problem with water because the pumps were not able to work without electricity, so we didn't only have a problem with water but also with the sewage system.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: You mentioned "they." You said "they." Who are they?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO LUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They -- the Muslims from Gradacac.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Where is Gradacac? Which direction is it in relation to Prud and Samac?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO LUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I orient myself properly, it's in the south, and it is about 24 or 25 kilometres away.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Can you please tell me whether there were any other activities that day aimed at resolving these, let me say, urgent problems with the civilian population? Did you make any kind of plan and agree on what you were going to do in the forthcoming period? What did this plan contain?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO LUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The main task was to try to restore peace amongst the population, if that was possible, to secure food, and when the electricity was cut off, to work on obtaining a power generator or generators. So the utility company, the electricity company did provide these power generators and they were used for the most vital institutions like the hospital, the sewage system, and the water supply. And the other facilities were left without electricity. We also tried to get some grocery stores to work. We tried to get them open so that the population could buy the necessary vital goods from there. Also, we had problems with shattered glass in windows and also damaged roofs, so that the civil defence system was already working on the repair of all of these things. The weather was bad. I remember that it was raining and snowing, so the civil protection service was already working on these roofs so that the people could have some kind of shelter and so that they would be able to live a bit more normally.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Could you please tell me according to earlier regulations, was it required of civilian officials to gather at certain places in case of emergency situations? Did you find out perhaps where your colleague -- Croats and Muslims were that day?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO LUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have to say that the law on defence regulated that matter. Every municipal official had his or her own wartime assignment, which mostly was located or had to do with his or her previous line of work. Therefore, I asked Mirko what the situation was and where were other officials who had their wartime assignments. However, he told me that some of them were not available, that there was an investigative procedure launched against some of them, and that that's why they were gone, and that those of us who were present had the duty to carry out both their tasks and tasks of those that were not there in order to keep the situation as normal as possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Please tell me, within the next following days, where was then the seat of the executive organs of the municipality?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO LUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the first couple of days - I can't tell you exactly whether it was two or three days - the seat was in the Pik company. And then after that, after the shelling of Pik started and the shelling of silos, where the wheat and corn were kept - and these were visible features in town and it was very easy for the other side, the Croatian side, to target these facilities - so they started shelling intensely that area and we had to move into another building. However, we still did not dare move to the municipal assembly building, and therefore we moved to the facilities of the state-owned company Uniglas. The reason for that was that the building was quite sturdy and it was more protected than other buildings in town.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: What steps were taken later on in order to organise civilian and municipal services in Uniglas? What services started functioning then and how did they cooperate among themselves?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO LUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as the executive council is concerned, in Uniglas there was president of the executive council, Mirko; assistant secretary for economy, Milan Simic; I, being the chief of the Internal Revenue Agency; and then Pero Bosic joined us, who was the director of the land surveyor agency. Since Mirko came and gave us tasks -- or rather, he gave to the Secretary for Economy the task of creating the plan for economy in wartime conditions, and therefore I joined Milan in creating the draft proposal for the decision on how to start the economy in wartime. Since Milan Simic was Assistant Secretary for Economy, and Lazar Mirkic was the secretary for economy, who did not come to work during those first few days because he worked on organising the economy and life in Pelagicevo and Donji Zabari.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for Mr. Pantelic, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Microphone, Mr. Pantelic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: I do apologise. Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let us go back to the structure of the executive council. You are now referring to the executive council of the Serbian Municipality of Bosanski Samac and Pelagicevo under formation, aren't you?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO LUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. At that time there was no other executive council in that area.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes. Ms. Registrar, could we have Exhibit D27/3. I believe it's a map of Samac. So we could swiftly check the positions of this premises. And also, Mr. Usher, could you arrange the transcript will be on the -- on the display in front of the witness, because then he can better follow the translation and then he can adjust his speed of speech.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On the ELMO, if you turn you'll be able to see what's placed on the ELMO. You have the pointer, and I would like to ask you to point out Pik company that you mentioned. Is it there?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO LUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Indicates]

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: It is. And then after that please show us where the Uniglas building was.

utterances.speaker: MIRKO LUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Indicates]

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Wait a minute. I am a bit confused now.

utterances.speaker: MIRKO LUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Oh, I apologise. Uniglas is here. Right here. Work organisation Uniglas, it's here.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes. Very well. Just one more question: Did the executive branch move to another building after Uniglas?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO LUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: After a few days of working in Uniglas, since there were no conditions for the executive council to work properly in that building due to other services such as archives and other services of the municipal assembly, Mirko Jovanovic and several other workers who worked in the administrative organs -- so all of us moved to the municipal building, the municipal assembly building.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Very well. Since on the map we can see two buildings, please tell us which one was the municipal building and what was in the other building.

utterances.speaker: MIRKO LUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The building marked with "SO" letters is the building of the municipal assembly, and the other one, marked with letters "SUP" is the police station, the Public Security Station.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Usher. In the meantime, could we have Exhibit P124. I believe that's the Official Gazette of Samac Municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sometime in late February, were you present when the Serbian Municipality of Bosanski Samac and Pelagicevo was created?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO LUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That was sometime in late February of 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Where was that meeting held?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO LUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was held in the memorial hall, the memorial hall called Mitar Trifunovic Uco.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Please tell me, do you know what was the basis for founding that Serbian Municipality of Bosanski Samac and Pelagicevo? Was that topic discussed?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO LUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was a recommendation coming from the presidency of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Since there was major outvoting going on, carried out by Muslim and Croat MPs, the recommendation was to establish Serbian municipalities, and I think that on the 29th of February, the Serbian Municipality of Bosanski Samac and Pelagicevo under formation was founded.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Just a tiny correction. Only if you know: Was that recommendation issued by the Presidency or the People's Assembly of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO LUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I remember, it was issued by the People's Assembly.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Could you please now turn to the second page of the Official Gazette. I assume that in the preamble it is stated why was that municipality founded.

utterances.speaker: MIRKO LUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It says here, "Based on the recommendation on the formation of the Municipal Assemblies of the Serbian People in Bosnia-Herzegovina," and this is the Official Gazette number 1/92.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: What did you say again? Could you repeat.

utterances.speaker: MIRKO LUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Pursuant to the recommendation on the formation of Municipal Assemblies of the Serbian People in Bosnia-Herzegovina."

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Very well. Now, please tell me, was there any discussion on establishing some organs as well, or were these organs elected later on? How did that first meeting held on the 29th of February, 1992 conclude?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO LUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The draft text of this decision was proposed, and as far as I remember, the president of the Serbian assembly was elected, together with the vice-president.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Very well. Who was the first president of the Serbian assembly, if you remember, please?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO LUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ilija Ristic. And the vice-president was Dusan Tanasic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: And the delegates at the assembly, were they members of only one or several political parties?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO LUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I remember, they were from several parties, not just one.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Do you remember what parties were those delegates members of?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO LUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were members of the Serb Democratic Party, SDP, and the Liberal Party.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Very well. Were you present at the second session of the Serb Assembly of Samac and Pelagicevo under assembly? We've already discussed the first. Now, were you present at the second session?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO LUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Do you remember whether at the second session an executive council was elected? Please turn to page 13, if I remember well.

utterances.speaker: MIRKO LUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Seven.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Seven. First, please take a look at the decision on appointing the executive council, and then tell us when did you learn of it.

utterances.speaker: MIRKO LUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I learned of it several days after this session of the assembly was held.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Were you present at any of the meetings held by that executive council from its founding until the 17th of April? Did you attend any of those meetings?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO LUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember that there were any meetings at all. I can see names here that I've never seen before on the executive council. I don't know these people today at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: All right. From that list of names, please tell us who was in the executive council and who did you work with from the 1st of April until July or August, or whenever it was.

utterances.speaker: MIRKO LUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mirko Jovanovic, Lazar Mirkic, I, Mirko Lukic. There were no other people.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: During 1992, was the executive council expanded together with the secretariat? Can you tell us, please, what fields were covered by what secretariat and who else was included in this executive branch of government, if I may call it that.

utterances.speaker: MIRKO LUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember that sometime in July or August Lazar Mirkic became president of the executive council in Brcko municipality, and his post was taken by Slobodan Sjencic, who became Secretary for Economy. In September, after the government of -- after the decree of the government of Republika Srpska, Secretariat for Housing and Utilities and Urban Affairs was established, and Veselin Blagojevic was appointed secretary. In September, again after a decree issued by the government of Republika Srpska, Secretariat for Social Affairs was established and Ilija Pavlovic was appointed secretary. Occasionally director of land surveying agency was included in the work as well. Pero Bosic, because he frequently had to go and perform his work obligation in the military, and then after that was completed, he would come back.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: You said that Pero Bosic had work obligation with the military. Do you know what exactly he did there? What was his occupation and what did he do in the military?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO LUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He's a qualified land surveyor, which means that he completed the relevant school at the university and he served as director of the municipal land surveying agency.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: But he was engaged by the army through a certain work duty. What did he do at that time, since you were colleagues? Do you know?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO LUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Occasionally he was attached to some military unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Very well. Did Milan Simic take up any post in the executive council? And if so, when? Just approximately. You don't need to know the exact date.

utterances.speaker: MIRKO LUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know precisely. In the beginning, Milan Simic was the Assistant Secretary for the Economy. And then on the 13th of May, 1992 he was elected as president of the executive council, because before that he -- actually, Mirko Jovanovic, who was the president of the executive council before him did -- was not performing that duty any more.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: And because of the transcript, what was that date that he was elected?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO LUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The 30th of May, 1992. The 30th.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: And what was your function at the time?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO LUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the time I was appointed as vice-president of the executive council, as well as the director of the municipal Internal Revenue Agency.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Usher. I am done for the moment with this exhibit. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could you please tell me: We understood that the bodies of the executive council grew as needed, as the pace of their duties grew. So could you please tell me, from April 1992 until the end of 1992, how many people approximately began working in those executive bodies? We're talking about April and May. And when I say that, I mean different expert services, different kind of jobs. I don't only mean the top officials. And could you please tell me how many people there were in these executive bodies at the end of 1992, approximately.

utterances.speaker: MIRKO LUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In those very first days in April, there were about 10 people, and this number by the end of the year grew. I cannot tell you exactly, but as far as I can recall, this number amounted to almost 30 -- between 20 and 30.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Very well. Could you please tell me: In the domain of organising the economy in wartime, what did the executive council undertake in this respect? And what kind of decisions did it make? So we just want a general idea, and we will go through individual decisions later. We just want the Trial Chamber to find something out from you about the general outlines and the things that were being done to develop the economy. What were the main tasks?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO LUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: After the decision of the Crisis Staff to declare a state of emergency, the economy was centralised and the Crisis Staff asked us, or asked the president of the executive council, and through the president down to us -- asked us to make a proposal for a decision about the work of the economy in wartime, which the Crisis Staff would adopt and verify. I remember that we, or the Secretariat for the Economy was directly charged with this task, but altogether we agreed at the executive council and proposed to the executive council what we saw, which economic subjects should continue to work in view of the situation that we had found ourselves in. The first task was to name coordinators in certain enterprises with the aim of forming the smallest possible work teams in their enterprises in order to preserve and protect the property and then to begin to work in those enterprises which were given permission to work.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Thank you. We will come back to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... Exhibit P89, please. Mr. Usher, please, can I check it just to be sure. Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could you please tell me, who made this decision that we are looking at right now?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO LUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Crisis Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: On what date?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO LUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The 19th of April, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: When did you personally find out about this decision?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO LUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that it was in the early evening hours of that same day.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Could you please tell me whether, based on this decision, did any activities begin by the municipal assembly's executive bodies, and could you please go back now to what you were saying about the further organisation of the economy, when we interrupted you to look at this decision.

utterances.speaker: MIRKO LUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. After this decision, the state of emergency was imposed. I think this was the first meeting of the Crisis Staff, and this was the first decision that was adopted. So since the state of emergency was imposed, the Crisis Staff made the decision that all institutional bodies in their present composition should stop their work, and it asked that its bodies or certain institutions that received permission from the staff can perform specific duties that they are qualified to carry out and that are in the interests or suit the needs of the Crisis Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... cannot follow what the witness was talking about if they don't receive B/C/S version on the ELMO. So could it be please placed on the ELMO, the B/C/S version, instead of English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. We've been through this before. But always when we are showing on the ELMO, the B/C/S version should be on the ELMO for the accused to follow.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Since you are a lawyer and you have been in state administrative bodies for a long time, could you please tell us what this term "Crisis Staff" stands for. What does it mean?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO LUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This question is regulated in accordance with principles from the constitution of Bosnia and Herzegovina and is regulated by subordinate regulations depending on the institution that they apply to. When we're talking about the municipal assembly, then in the statute of the municipal assembly it's regulated there. The term "crisis" means that it's some kind of emergency state or emergency situation that is not normal or is not the way that it was before, and that because of that, certain measures have to be taken in order to overcome such a situation and bring affairs back to normal. And this definition -- this term "Crisis Staff" is contained in the statute of the municipal assembly in case of emergency situations, such as floods, earthquakes, and ultimately war.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Do you have any personal knowledge that in that period in 1992 there was a Croat Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO LUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I heard that a Crisis Staff was formed in Prud, but I don't think that it was purely Croatian. I think that there were also representatives of the Muslims or Bosniaks there too.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: The question was: Do you have any personal knowledge in the period, and the witness basically speculated as to whether there was one, a Croat Crisis Staff.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. Because it's -- yes. He doesn't appear to have personal knowledge.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Do you personally know, perhaps, whether there was a Crisis Staff in Slavonski Samac, Domaljevac, in Odzak, in Gradacac?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO LUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Crisis Staff in Prud was something that I discussed with Mr. Sulejman Tihic. I don't know about Crisis Staffs. I don't have any personal knowledge regarding Slavonski Samac or some other places.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: For example, in the month of May, did you hear that there was a Crisis Staff in Odzak? I'm thinking now of a Croatian Crisis Staff.

utterances.speaker: MIRKO LUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: So more or less each side had its own form of this body; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I objected to that. That's --

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: I withdraw. I withdraw.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could you please tell me, what -- who did the Crisis Staff represent?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO LUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If we're talking about the assembly -- the municipality, it stood in for the municipal assembly, for the deputies of the municipal assembly.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... I do apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And could you please tell me, how long did this body, the Crisis Staff, operate for? How long was it active?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO LUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There is no specific time period. It lasts or operates for as long as the situation is brought back to normal or until some higher law resolves that question.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Specifically, in Samac do you know whether at some point during 1992 did another body come about? Was another body introduced as a replacement for the Crisis Staff, if you know?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO LUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember that sometime in the summer - I don't know whether it was July or August - the term "Crisis Staff" was substituted by the term "War Presidency" at the proposal of the National Assembly of Republika Srpska in accordance with a decision of that assembly.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Very well. And when did the parliament or the Municipal Assembly of Bosanski Samac begin to function?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO LUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I remember, according to the decision of the National Assembly, War Presidencies were supposed to work instead of the municipal assembly for as long as they felt that conditions were not created in order to be able to establish normal life in the territory of that municipality, which means that depending on the situation, the War Presidency was the one to decide whether it was possible again to have civilian institutions work normally in the territory of the assembly.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: And when if a situation like that ever happened, when did the Municipal Assembly of Bosanski Samac begin to function?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO LUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that in mid-December 1992 the first meeting was convened of that body after the Crisis Staff and the War Presidency. This meeting was convened by the -- or called for by the War Presidency.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Did the executive council as a body have any kind of obligation before this assembly was convened, in terms of informing or preparing this? Could you give me some details about that. What did you in accordance with the statute have to do as a body in order to -- or before this meeting of the municipal assembly was convened?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO LUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as the executive council is concerned, all the things that were done by the executive council had to be verified by this assembly, and the president of the executive council was tasked with preparing a report on the work of the executive council and this report contained the reports on the work of each secretariat or administrative sector of the executive council.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: When we are on this topic, could you please tell me, during the state of war - and I'm talking about the period of 1992 and 1993 - what was the relationship of certain municipal secretariats and higher bodies and the appropriate ministries? Could you please give us an explanation of how this functioned during the war.

utterances.speaker: MIRKO LUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is how it was organised: The government of Republika Srpska had its ministries. The Minister for Industry, then the Secretary for Economy was subordinated to the minister at the municipal level. The Minister of Finance had as a subordinate at the municipal level the Director of the Internal Revenue Agency. The Minister for education and health had at the municipal level subordinated to him the secretary for social affairs. The director of the republican land surveying and property affairs at the municipal level had below him the director of the land surveying agency and property affairs. So the structure of the executive council reflected the structure of the government, and the powers of each one were commensurate. The municipal bodies were responsible to the higher minister bodies.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: What regulations are passed by the relevant ministry in Republika Srpska and do they have a mandatory character for the relevant bodies at the municipal level?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO LUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In peacetime, they pass laws; and in wartime, they pass decrees. Therefore, the government -- or rather, the ministries pass decrees with the force of law, and they also pass decisions and instructions which are regulations meant to implement these decrees. And they are mandatory for relevant municipal organs.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: In practice, when these decrees are implemented, is there a previous consent of the municipal assembly needed in order to implement these decrees? Please tell us, how does this system work?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO LUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It depends on the enactment or the decree passed by the government regulating certain matters. There are such decrees which are mandatory, and then there are decrees which specify that the municipal organ needs to pass further regulations and therefore -- and then give a recommendation regarding that to the municipal assembly, which then adopts a relevant regulation. I can give you an example from my field. For example, the Ministry of Finance can say that an income tax can be, let's say, between 1 and 3 per cent, and then the Internal Revenue Agency prepares draft decision and says in Samac the income tax will be 2 per cent and then the municipal assembly -- or rather, its assemblymen vote on this. They can either adopt the proposal of 2 per cent or they can change the figure, but the figure cannot be higher than 3 per cent or lower than 1 per cent, which was regulated by the Ministry of Finance.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: And when there is no municipal assembly -- for example, in wartime in 1992 -- which organ acts instead of the municipal assembly in these matters?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO LUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The War Presidency.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: All right. Now, tell me this, please: If the government passes a decision on work obligation, is this decision applied directly? If so, by whom? Or does this decision need to be ratified or verified at the local level? By this, I mean the municipal assembly. If you know, how did this work in reality?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO LUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, the decree on the work obligation, it did not give any authorities to anyone else. It clearly specified that the Secretariat for National Defence regulated these matters and that it implemented decisions or acts passed by the relevant ministry of the government. Therefore, the municipal assembly, the Crisis Staffs, and the War Presidencies had no powers regarding adding or changing something in these regulations.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: What about the war economy? What about the economy in wartime? What happened when the relevant Ministry of Republika Srpska passed an enactment in this field? Would the same rules that you told us apply in this case as well?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO LUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: What about the abandoned property, apartments, houses, abandoned in wartime?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO LUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The ministries passed decrees which specified the manner, conditions, and criteria under which the municipal organ had to further implement these decrees.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Excuse me. Mr. Lukic, would you be able to recall how "abandoned property" was defined in those rules, if you can, if you have knowledge of that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The decree specified clearly what constituted abandoned property, whether it was publicly-owned apartments -- or rather, state-owned apartments or privately-owned houses, or agricultural land and facilities on that agricultural land which then had the status of abandoned property.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: In order to better assist the Trial Chamber, could we have Exhibit D18/2, please. Because in fact, that's a decree and we can have interpretation.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please take a look at this decree and tell us who passed it. It's to your right. Please take a look at it.

utterances.speaker: MIRKO LUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The government of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina adopted the decree --

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Please turn to the last page of this decree and tell us the date. It's on the last page. And I believe there are three pages.

utterances.speaker: MIRKO LUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: 30th of July, 1992. Signed by the prime minister, Dr. Branko Djeric. This decree deals -- or regulates the temporary usage of facilities -- housing facilities and commercial premises.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us what falls under this decree, what kind of facilities.

utterances.speaker: MIRKO LUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it's specified here under Article 2. Every decree had to specify what was regulated by it, and here in Article 2 it says that these were -- the following facilities could be given for temporary use. These were housing facilities, state-owned, catering and tourist facilities, residential houses, apartments, vacation homes, and then commercial premises in state, private, or mixed ownership, provided they were empty and abandoned.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: All right. Now, could you please give us your interpretation of paragraph 2 under Article 2, because this one regulates apartments that had not been abandoned. What cases were those?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO LUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Apartments which had not been abandoned can be used or, rather, given into temporary use in order to accommodate people, providing that the owner or the tenant had extra housing premises mentioned in Article 6 of this decree. Let me tell you how this was applied in practice.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: I believe it's time for a break, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. We'll take our break and continue at 16.15 hours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Pantelic, you're continuing.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Your Honour. Could we have Exhibit D18/2, that we have discussed prior to the break. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Briefly, Article 6 of this decree discusses the kinds of apartments and number of household members. Is that what the Article 6 speaks about?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO LUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: All right. Since that's a little bit unusual, please tell us, how is it if somebody is already living in an apartment or in a house that has several hundred square metres, how was it possible to regulate through a decree and to have somebody else move into the same premises where other persons are already living? Could you please explain that to us. We knew that that was wartime and there were certain problems, but can you tell us what reasons were behind this decree.

utterances.speaker: MIRKO LUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is difficult for me to say what the real reasons the government had when it passed this decision, but I can tell you what general reasons could have been. There was a terrible problem on the ground because a lot of houses had been destroyed through shelling and a lot of people were homeless. We also had a lot of refugees that poured in all municipalities and they also had no shelter in the municipalities where they found themselves in; therefore, the motive of the government and the competent ministry was to through a decree specify how these matters should be resolved at the municipal level, because on one hand, there were a number of housing facilities that were vacant, and there were such families that had extra housing space, and on the other hand, there were such families that didn't have a roof above their heads. Therefore, a decree was passed and criteria were established to regulate this and then it was set forth that relevant municipal organs had to take certain steps in order to implement this.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Do you know whether in some other entities of Bosnia and Herzegovina these matters were regulated in a similar way? Do you know about that?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO LUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. After the war, I had an occasion to contact my colleagues from those areas, and then I realised that this issue was regulated in a similar or identical way.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: I'm just giving you an example. If somebody had two houses on one piece of land, would that person have to take in, into one of those two houses, people who were homeless?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO LUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: In Samac municipality, were there any discriminatory procedures? Namely, was this principle applied to each resident regardless of his or her ethnicity or were there some modalities in the way that this was applied?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO LUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know of any discriminatory cases. I know that people of all ethnicities asked for housing space on one hand, and then on the other hand there were Muslim, Croats, and Serbs who had extra housing space. And houses were -- or housing was provided to people of all three ethnicities. If a shell destroyed a house of a Muslim or a Serb or a Croat, we couldn't just leave that person in the street. Those who were in charge of housing policies had to provide housing for that person on a temporary basis. This was not a long-term solution, and this didn't touch into ownership matters. This was just a temporary measure that had to provide temporary housing for homeless people. We would issue a decision allotting somebody housing space for one year with a proviso that in case this person failed to find a long-term solution, then the validity of this decision could be extended until such time.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: And for example, if there was a refugee who was given temporary use of an apartment or a part of a house - now I'm referring to Serb refugees specifically - would these refugees be able to acquire property rights to somebody else's apartment or house via this mechanism?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO LUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. There was no legal basis to allow something of that nature. Therefore, none of these people could have acquired property rights to the property which was given to them for temporary use. Now we have the process of restitution of houses all set up and real estate is currently being returned to their original owners.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: I assume that this process is taking place on the entire territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina, in both entities.

utterances.speaker: MIRKO LUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If it means anything to you, the average of restitution of a property in Bosnia and Herzegovina is 65 per cent, and in Samac that percentage is around 90 per cent, so property is being returned to its rightful owners. So in Samac the percentage is over 90 per cent, while in Bosnia and Herzegovina in both entities this figure is around 65 per cent.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: I just have one other question on this point. Mr. Lukic, if a person had been taken into detention in the TO or the SUP, for example, and that person had locked the door of their apartment, been taken into detention, and then did not return to that apartment because that person was exchanged, would that have been classified as abandoned property?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The apartment did have the status of an abandoned property under this regulation, and then the municipal body would form a commission which would go out in the field and it would bring in another family to that house or apartment. It would make a report about the property and things that were in the apartment or house at the time and would archive this report. The property where another family was brought in did not belong to that family; neither did the things that were inside that property, did they belong to this other family.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Thank you. And just one supplementary question: From what you've just said, Mr. Lukic, there was a procedure for taking an inventory of the movable property inside of the apartment and presumably that was held by the requisite municipal office.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. The Department for Housing and Communal Affairs. They were the ones who would implement and oversee the implementation of that regulation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, while we're on this topic and in terms of the question asked by Judge Williams, could you please read Article 12. Could you please read Article 12 aloud.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters do not have a copy of the document.

utterances.speaker: MIRKO LUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Abandoned property will be considered as that property if the user or owner of that space does not return within 30 days from the day after which circumstances and due to which the owner originally had to leave the property." Yes. This is just what I spoke about.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Usher. I'm finished with that. Yes. Could we have Exhibit P3, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could you please look at this document, Mr. Lukic. Look through it. Could you please read the title.

utterances.speaker: MIRKO LUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Instructions for the organisation and activity of the organs of the Serbian people in Bosnia and Herzegovina in extraordinary circumstances. Sarajevo, December 19th, 1991."

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Did you personally ever see this document before or a copy of that document?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO LUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I am seeing this material for the first time.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Did you ever hear in Samac that a document with this title was discussed or that any measures were taken in accordance with this document?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO LUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Usher. Could we have Exhibit P37, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What is this document, please?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO LUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is the list of employees who were on work obligation. Their names are stated here, the number of days that they spent on working obligation, and the amount of the salary that they received for that number of days in accordance with established coefficients.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: What was the role of the executive council in the implementation in regard to these salaries. Could you please explain the mechanism to us, please, briefly.

utterances.speaker: MIRKO LUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The executive council or the person who was in charge of the budget had the task of paying out salaries to all of those who were on the list or all of those who were on the budget. They were members of the Crisis Staff. They were members of the executive council, the civil defence, and the work obligation.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Just one question: When the executive council approves in accordance with the budget constrains a certain amount, what happens next? Does the executive council pay that out from its own treasury, or is there some other financial arrangement whereby this transaction is carried out?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO LUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: One of the first tasks that I had as the director of the Internal Revenue Agency was to establish a payment system, to make such a system function, because at that time we had problems because our service for payments was carrying its work through the branch in Modrica and because we were not able to do our usual things because the communications were disrupted between Samac and Modrica, we had to establish payments through the branch office in Bijeljina, and this is how that system worked. What does that mean? The funds on the budget account were in the service for payment agency, and then these funds -- I can't see whether it's 84 or 34 thousand -- would then be transferred to the Privredna bank and these names and all other names that would be on the payroll lists from the budget would then go to the bank and they would withdraw or cash the amount that was stated on the payroll list, which was passed down from the payment agency for payment.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: And where was this bank located? Where was the headquarters of that bank?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO LUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was in the town, in Samac.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... Mr. Usher, thank you. I've finished with that document.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Mr. Pantelic, could you repeat the number of the document. It's not on the transcript. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Yes. This is P76.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could you please tell me whether you have any personal knowledge about the special purposes battalion of the Army of Republika Srpska of Bosnia and Herzegovina. Do you have any information about who was their commander and other details?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO LUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, since I was not in the army, the battalion comprised some 4 to 5 hundred soldiers. These were boys from the territory of our municipality who occasionally were given assignments. These were usually younger men who did not want to go out to the line, the separation line between the two sides. But in case this line was broken through at some points, they would then join the unit that would go and return the part of the line that was broken to its original state. So all the battalions were manned by men from the territory of our municipality. And as far as who the commander was, I know it was Milan Josic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Where is Milan Josic from?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO LUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From Obudovac.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: So Obudovac is in that area?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO LUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It's a local community in our municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Were there any other soldiers in that battalion who were not from the territory of the Samac municipality?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO LUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Excuse me. Go ahead. I thought that you wanted to say something, so I didn't want to interrupt you.

utterances.speaker: MIRKO LUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wanted to say I'm not sure, but I think that there were volunteers there, about 10 or 15 of them, who were part of the 2nd Posavina Infantry Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: And do you happen to know what was the objective of this decision to obtain uniforms? What was the motivation for the decision? Upon whose request were the uniforms procured? And then could you please tell us why this was done, if you know.

utterances.speaker: MIRKO LUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do. The request was issued by the Crisis Staff. It approved the procurement of 500 uniforms. And the motive was because all these men were in different uniforms and in such operations, they could not recognise or distinguish one another. Some were wearing multicoloured uniforms. Some were wearing different kinds of uniforms. So the idea was for them to look like real soldiers, to be uniformed and to all have the same uniform. Some didn't even have uniforms.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Do you know whether this was a decision at the initiative of the Crisis Staff, or did they receive a request from someone else in this matter, if you know?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO LUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When we're talking about logistics of the army, the request was issued by the brigade command, so I think that this request was probably along the same lines as the others.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Usher. Can we have now Exhibit P88, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Lukic, could you please tell me -- this is an order by the Crisis Staff, is it not?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO LUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is an order issued on the 24th of April, 1992 by the Crisis Staff. I remember this order. The president of the executive council came; that was Mirko Jovanovic then. And he asked the Secretariat for Economy to prepare this order for the Crisis Staff because there were some cases where some individuals had started appropriating some things, things that they had found, and taking them to their houses. Military police or civilian police at the checkpoints would stop them, and since proceedings were initiated afterwards, they had to find a location to store these items until the completion of the proceedings. Therefore, the Secretariat for Economy prepared this decision for the Crisis Staff -- there is a mistake in this decision. The warehouse was not located in Bosanac company in Obudovac, but rather it was differently called and it wasn't the premises of Uniglas, as mentioned here, but rather the premises of Utva in Bosanski Samac. These were two warehouses where these goods were stored until the completion of the proceedings. As is stated here, the motive was to stop war profiteering and personal gain of certain individuals.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: So instead of the company called DD Bosanac, it should be something else.

utterances.speaker: MIRKO LUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It should be ZZ Obudovac, standing for agricultural cooperative in Obudovac. And then it should be a DP Utva which stands for "state-owned enterprise" in Bosanski Samac.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: If you look at the signature, does this look like the signature of Dr. Blagoje Simic? I assume that you are familiar with his signature.

utterances.speaker: MIRKO LUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No, I cannot recognise whose signature this is.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: But as far as known to you, the executive council made this draft decision through the Secretariat for Economy; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO LUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. I read this decision when it was prepared, and it was prepared by the Secretariat for Economy, to be presented at the Crisis Staff and the Secretary for Economy was supposed to present this order and then the Crisis Staff was supposed to adopt it.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: And based on what you know, can you tell us the basis for this order or decision. Was it to legalise plundering or prevent plundering?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO LUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The objective was to prevent individuals from plundering and acquiring illegal personal gain.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Usher. Could we have now, please, Exhibit P100.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please take a look at this decision, Mr. Lukic. It is rather self-explanatory. I would like you to comment on Article 2 of this decision. I would like to know what a person with your background and knowledge can tell us about the aim, the purpose of this Article 2 of this decision.

utterances.speaker: MIRKO LUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I know this decision. The purpose of the decision, as I've just told you, was that we had to link certain activities with Bijeljina. One of such activities was the agency for payment systems. That further means that all of those who couldn't execute their tasks in a normal way had to find an alternative solution. Within SAO Semberija and Majevica, these matters were regulated, and therefore we had to base our activities on theirs, depending on whether they had some direct or indirect links with us.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: The decisions of SAO Semberija and Majevica from the sphere of their competences naturally, were these decisions mandatory for your municipality and your municipal organs?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO LUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, there was no decisions whatsoever, because this matter was very soon thereafter regulated at the level of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina. Therefore, this institution did not pass any enactments, nor did it make it compulsory for us to implement them. The army was already connected to the troops in Bijeljina. The payment services were regulated as well through the branch office in Modrica. Once the corridor with Modrica was established again, then things went back to normal, so that after the month of June we had no further contacts with Semberija.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: And whom did you have contacts with then?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO LUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Since the entire territory was functioning properly, that means we had a relationship with the government and government organs on the ground, and naturally with the People's Assembly. That's who we had contacts with.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Could we have now Exhibit P102. 102, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please tell me briefly what you can about this decision. First of all, tell us which organ drafted this decision to be adopted by the Crisis Staff on the 13th of June.

utterances.speaker: MIRKO LUKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The draft of this decision was prepared by the executive council and delivered to the Crisis Staff to be adopted.
